title: Still Water
scene: The things they agree to do tomorrow.

paragraphs: They ate at the table. The invitations were on the windowsill, the damp one drying on its own.
Halfway through dinner she looked towards the paintings and stopped chewing.
He pushed the water a little closer. She swallowed and finished the mouthful.
Her father sent another message. "Call whenever. We will be at the shop."
She wrote that the exhibition had been canceled and that she would explain in the morning. She read it to Mukund before sending it.
She sent it before she could change anything.
For a minute she kept the phone in her hand. Then she laid it down.
They cleared the table. She wrote the transport refund on the back of an envelope; he put it beside her notebook. The wet invitation had begun to curl at one corner.
At eleven, he told her someone had replied about a venue.
He closed the laptop and put it in his bag.
Aarna was on the sofa with her feet tucked beneath her. He moved a cushion and sat down.
He picked at a loose thread on his cuff.
She rested her hand between them, not quite touching his.
"I didn't like the way you spoke to me," he said.
"But I can't do the part where I think you're leaving," she said.
"Next time I need a minute, I'll say where I'm going."
She shifted her hand against his.
"Are we going to act like this was just the gallery?"
"Will you talk to me about it when I'm not crying?"
She looked down at their hands.
"I want you here," she said. "I just..."
He turned his hand beneath hers.
After a while, she asked whether he had listened to his mother's recording.
He sent his mother a message saying he would listen in the morning. Then he moved his bag from beside the door to the sofa.
The invitation slid out when he fetched his charger.
She picked it up before he could. It was flat and clean, protected inside a folded product sheet.
She gave it back. He put it where it had been.
At eleven forty-two, she switched off the bright light above the table. Only the lamp beside the sofa remained.
The paper with the cross lay on the floor. The hammer was still on the windowsill.
She made room for him and rested her head against his shoulder. His arm was at the wrong angle; her hair caught under his collar. They adjusted.
A train passed at the end of the block. The teaspoon in her empty cup rattled once.
Across the room, the pale doorway in her painting was just visible.
He asked whether she wanted the lamp off.
